title: Libraries and Utilities
readerIntent: Decide whether reusable code belongs in a capability library, shared utility, or service.
owner: Owning capability or nCommon for genuinely framework-wide primitives
summary: Libraries and utilities provide small explicit mechanics; they never become hidden homes for business logic, provider selection, configuration loading, or runtime state.

sections.heading: What is Libraries and Utilities?
paragraphs: A library provides reusable code for a defined capability, while a utility performs a small broadly useful technical task. Correct placement matters because shared code can otherwise create hidden coupling, duplicate authority, or dependencies that every module must carry.

Think of specialist tools stored with the team that owns them and truly general tools stored in a common workshop. A tool should move to the common workshop only when several independent teams need the same stable behavior.

sections.heading: Placement rule
items: Keep capability-specific helpers beside the owning capability.
Use nCommon only for stable framework-wide deterministic primitives.
Use a service when behavior needs configuration, I/O, state, policy, providers, or business meaning.
Pass tenant, request, module, correlation, and execution context explicitly.

sections.heading: Risks of casual sharing
items: A shared helper becomes a widely consumed compatibility contract.
Hidden I/O or globals make testing, override, security, and performance unpredictable.
Moving code merely to shorten an import path erases ownership.
A second utility, enum, error, or status registry creates parallel authority.

sections.heading: Library, utility, or service
items: Use a pure utility for deterministic transformation with explicit inputs and outputs.
Use a capability library for cohesive reusable mechanics owned by that capability.
Use a service for configuration, I/O, state, policy, provider access, business meaning, or lifecycle.
Use a provider adapter for vendor-specific behavior behind a neutral contract.
Do not use a utility to avoid proper dependency injection or module ownership.

sections.heading: Examples
paragraphs: Safe examples include bounded string normalization, object-path handling, date parsing with explicit locale, or error-cause helpers. These operations do not choose a tenant, open a connection, or decide business permission.
Employee activation, cache access, database queries, token issuance, provider selection, and configuration loading are services or owned capabilities, not common utilities.

sections.heading: Compatibility responsibility
paragraphs: A framework-wide helper can have hundreds of consumers. Changes to input tolerance, mutation, errors, ordering, Unicode, time zones, or performance can create broad regressions.
Keep the contract narrow, document edge cases, avoid hidden globals, and test representative consumers before changing shared behavior.

sections.heading: Security and performance
items: Never serialize or log credentials for convenience.
Do not accept unbounded recursion, collections, regular expressions, or payloads.
Avoid prototype mutation and unsafe object merging.
Preserve safe cause and correlation without copying sensitive context.
Measure allocation and latency for helpers on high-volume paths.

sections.heading: Review checklist
items: Existing helper and owner searched.
More than one genuine consumer identified.
Inputs, outputs, mutation, errors, complexity, and compatibility documented.
No I/O, provider, secret, tenant selection, or business authority hidden.
Boundary, security, concurrency, performance, and consumer tests present.
